summary: For ages 10–11: solving problems whose answers must be rounded to a specified degree of accuracy, AND deciding the sensible degree of accuracy from context. Two intertwined skills: (i) rounding a computed result to a stated place using the deciding digit (e.g. 3.6875 to 1 d.p. → 3.7), and (ii) judging from the situation when the plain nearest-value rule must be overridden — round UP for 'how many are needed/enough' (3.2 containers → 4), round DOWN for 'how many complete whole units', keep to the penny for money, keep whole for counts of people. Keep full precision through multi-step work and round only at the end.
misconceptions: Applying the nearest-value rule when context demands rounding up ('need 3.2 buses' → answering 3 instead of 4) or down ('how many whole boxes fill' → rounding up wrongly).
Rounding at intermediate steps and accumulating error into the final answer.
Rounding to the wrong place, or using the wrong deciding digit (looking two places along).
Giving impossible precision for the context (money to 3dp, a count of people as a decimal).
Truncating (chopping digits) instead of rounding, e.g. 3.68 to 1dp given as 3.6.

activities.title: Round it right: scenarios where the rounding move has consequences
steps: Compute a problem that yields a raw decimal, e.g. 80 people needing 15-seat buses: 80 ÷ 15 = 5.33 (to 2 d.p.).
Choose a rounding move — round to the nearest whole, round down, or round up — and, where relevant, to which place.
Play out or describe the result of your choice in the situation: rounding to the nearest whole (5 buses) seats only 75 and leaves 5 people stranded at the kerb; rounding up to 6 buses seats everyone.
State in words why context (needing to carry everyone), not the deciding digit, forces rounding up here: the deciding digit (the 3 in 5.33) would round down to 5, yet the situation needs 6.
Repeat with a 'round down' context, e.g. 'How many complete 50 cm lengths can be cut from 3.4 m?' 340 ÷ 50 = 6.8 → 6 complete lengths, not 7, even though 6.8 is nearer to 7.
Repeat with a 'nearest' context where the plain rule does apply, e.g. 'round 47 ÷ 6 to one decimal place' → 7.8.
activities.insight: The context — what the answer is used for — decides whether you round up, down, or to the nearest, and this can override the mechanical nearest-value rule.

activities.title: Number-line rounder for the pure mechanic
steps: Mark the raw answer on a number line between the two candidate rounded values, with the midpoint shown.
Identify the digit being rounded and the deciding digit immediately to its right.
Decide which candidate the value is nearer to and round to it.
Deliberately contrast rounding with truncating: show that 3.68 to 1 d.p. is 3.7, NOT 3.6 (chopping).
activities.insight: Nearest-value rounding is justified by position on the number line and the single deciding digit; truncating (chopping digits) is a different, incorrect move.

activities.title: Money and measures: choosing a sensible degree of accuracy
steps: For a money result, round to the nearest penny (2 d.p.) and explain why 3 d.p. is not sensible for pounds and pence.
For a measurement context, round to the stated accuracy, e.g. nearest tenth of a second.
For a count of people, give a whole number and explain why a decimal count is impossible.
For each context, answer the question: 'Does this level of accuracy make sense here, and what will the answer be used for?'
activities.insight: The appropriate degree of accuracy is a purposeful decision set by the context and the use of the answer, not an arbitrary number of decimal places.

activities.title: Sort the problems: up, down, or nearest
steps: Read a set of word problems and sort each into 'round up', 'round down', or 'round to nearest'.
For each, write the reason in words (e.g. 'need enough to fit everyone' → up; 'how many complete' → down; 'to the nearest tenth' → nearest).
Then solve two or three and carry out the move you sorted it into.
activities.insight: Children should choose the rounding move by the meaning of the problem, not by habit.

activities.title: Round at the end, not in the middle
steps: Work a multi-step calculation twice: once rounding each intermediate value early, once keeping full precision and rounding only the final answer.
Compare the two final answers and describe whether and how early rounding changed the result (choose numbers where it does, so the effect is visible).
State the rule: keep precision through the steps, round last.
activities.insight: Rounding at intermediate steps can accumulate error; rounding only the final answer protects accuracy.

activities.title: Justify-the-accuracy discussion
steps: Given a real situation posed aloud, say whether you would round up, down, or to the nearest, and why, BEFORE the outcome is revealed.
Answer probing questions: 'Why round UP to 6 coaches even though 5.2 is nearer 5?'; 'If the question asked for the nearest whole number instead of coaches needed, would your answer change?'
Defend your chosen degree of accuracy in words.
activities.insight: Being able to justify the accuracy decision in context — and recognising that re-wording the question can change the correct move — shows command of the objective.

checkQuestion: Give the child problems where the rounding decision matters and watch how they round the RESULT: 'Work out 47 ÷ 6 and give the answer to one decimal place'; and a context one — '260 people travel in coaches holding 50 each. How many coaches are needed?' Watch whether they round by the rule when asked, but round UP for whole coaches regardless of the decimal.
checkAnswer: 47 ÷ 6 = 7.83..., to 1 d.p. = 7.8. Coaches: 260 ÷ 50 = 5.2, but you need 6 coaches (the 0.2 of a coach still carries people, so round UP). The teacher watches for correct rounding-rule application AND context-driven rounding that overrides the rule when whole units are required.
